Nearby galaxies offer a unique window to study these processes in detail and with high spatial resolution. The $μ$Jy sensitivity, sub-arcsecond angular resolution and broadband coverage provided by SKA AA4 configuration will enable us to separate morphologically and spectrally the contribution from SMBH accretion and star formation processes, from the most compact nuclear region out to the most diffuse, galaxy-wide components. Disentangling thermal and non-thermal emission using multi-scale spectral index maps (traced by SKA-Mid) and absorption processes (traced mainly by SKA-Low) will allow us to account for the present and past star-formation rate, the AGN activity and the ISM properties. SKA observations of a wide range of galaxy types in the nearby Universe, including quiescent, AGN-dominated and starburst galaxies, will provide a broad view of how star formation and accretion regulate galaxy evolution, while time-domain and spectral-variability information further isolate compact accretion and transient phenomena.

AI.tldr: The SKA AA4 configuration's high sensitivity, resolution, and broadband coverage will enable detailed separation of star formation and supermassive black hole accretion processes in nearby galaxies via multi-scale spectral and absorption mapping, providing insights into galaxy evolution.
AI.motivation: Galaxy appearance is dominated by two key physical phenomena: star formation and accretion onto supermassive black holes. Nearby galaxies offer a unique opportunity to study these processes at high spatial resolution, but current observations lack the sensitivity and broadband coverage to fully disentangle their contributions across different spatial scales.
AI.method: Use SKA AA4 configuration ($μ$Jy sensitivity, sub-arcsecond angular resolution, broadband coverage) to separate morphological and spectral contributions of SMBH accretion and star formation via multi-scale spectral index maps (SKA-Mid) and absorption processes (SKA-Low), across nuclear to galaxy-wide components.
AI.result: SKA will disentangle thermal and non-thermal emission, enabling measurement of present/past star-formation rate, AGN activity, and ISM properties, while providing a broad view across quiescent, AGN-dominated, and starburst galaxies, with time-domain and spectral-variability isolating compact accretion and transient phenomena.
AI.conclusion: SKA observations will provide a comprehensive understanding of how star formation and accretion regulate galaxy evolution in the nearby Universe.

title: When Jets Don't Quench: Near-Infrared H$_{2}$ in Star Forming Low-Excitation Radio Galaxies
summary: We present new Gemini/GNIRS near-infrared spectroscopic observations of eight low-redshift ($z < 0.1$) blue low-excitation radio galaxies (BLERGs), a rare subset ($\sim 2.5\%$ of low-excitation radio galaxies; LERGs) that complicate the classical jet-mode AGN picture by combining radio activity with star-forming, gas-rich hosts. These star-forming BLERGs exhibit significant warm H$_2$ emission traced via ro-vibrational transitions at $T \sim 2000$--$4000$ K. We find that BLERGs span a broad range of mass-normalized warm H$_2$ luminosities ($L_{\rm H_2}/M_\star$), comparable to radio-emitting early-type galaxies, yet without a clear positive dependence on radio power. Instead, the strongest H$_2$ emission preferentially occurs in morphologically disturbed and advanced-merger systems, while compact radio sources ($\lesssim 20$ kpc) remain plausible sites of localized jet-ISM interaction. Together, these results suggest that merger-driven processes, including tidal shocks, gas inflows, and disturbed interstellar medium conditions, are the dominant drivers of warm molecular gas excitation in BLERGs, although localized jet-driven heating may contribute in individual systems. The compact radio morphologies, gas-rich hosts, and rarity of BLERGs are consistent with a short-lived evolutionary phase in which radio AGN activity coexists with an interaction-driven, molecular-rich interstellar medium prior to the onset of large-scale maintenance-mode feedback. Spatially resolved spectroscopy and higher-resolution radio imaging will be essential to disentangle the relative roles of mergers and jets in regulating the molecular gas of jet-mode AGN.

AI.tldr: This study presents near-infrared spectroscopy of eight blue low-excitation radio galaxies (BLERGs), finding that their warm H₂ emission is primarily driven by merger-related processes (tidal shocks, gas inflows, disturbed ISM) rather than jet activity, suggesting BLERGs represent a short-lived evolutionary phase bridging merger-driven gas-rich hosts and mature jet-mode feedback.
AI.motivation: BLERGs are a rare (~2.5%) subset of LERGs that complicate the classical jet-mode AGN picture by hosting both radio activity and star-forming, gas-rich hosts. Understanding their molecular gas excitation mechanisms is crucial for clarifying the interplay between jets, mergers, and feedback in these systems.
AI.method: The authors used new Gemini/GNIRS near-infrared spectroscopy to observe eight low-redshift (z<0.1) BLERGs, measuring ro-vibrational H₂ transitions at T~2000-4000 K to derive warm H₂ luminosities and compare with radio power, stellar mass, and morphological properties.
AI.result: BLERGs span a broad range of mass-normalized warm H₂ luminosities comparable to radio-emitting early-type galaxies, but without a clear positive correlation with radio power. Strongest H₂ emission is found in morphologically disturbed/advanced-merger systems, while compact radio sources (≤20 kpc) may allow localized jet-ISM interaction.
AI.conclusion: Merger-driven processes (tidal shocks, gas inflows, disturbed ISM) are the dominant drivers of warm H₂ excitation in BLERGs, though localized jet heating may contribute in some cases. BLERGs likely represent a short-lived evolutionary phase before large-scale maintenance-mode feedback establishes. Spatially resolved spectroscopy and higher-resolution radio imaging are needed to disentangle the roles of mergers and jets.

title: SKA$-$VLBI view of AGN jets in the early Universe
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Spingola01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are among the brightest sources in the Universe, and those that are also jetted are uniquely valuable at the earliest epochs, because their relativistic outflows can regulate the gas supply of their host galaxies, potentially affecting both early star formation and the rapid growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs). Their compact, high-brightness-temperature radio cores provide the sharpest beacons for very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), enabling direct constraints on Doppler boosting, jet duty cycles, and jet$-$environment coupling at extreme redshifts. In this White Paper, we discuss how the SKA-VLBI will provide sub-$μ$Jy sensitivity together with milliarcsecond (mas) angular resolution to image and characterise jetted AGN at $z>6$ across SKA-Mid and SKA-Low frequencies. These observations can directly test SMBHs ($>10^6$ M$_{\odot}$) formation/evolution models (including jet-assisted super-Eddington phases) and infer the geometry of the Universe, directly probing the cosmological framework at high precision. Synergies with current and next-generation multi-band facilities will also be crucial to fully understand their host galaxies and their environment, providing an unprecedented panchromatic knowledge of the first jetted AGN.

AI.tldr: This White Paper discusses how SKA-VLBI will provide sub-μJy sensitivity and milliarcsecond resolution to image jetted AGN at z>6, enabling direct tests of SMBH formation/evolution models, constraints on cosmology, and studies of jet-environment coupling at extreme redshifts.
AI.motivation: Jetted AGN at high redshifts (z>6) are uniquely valuable because their relativistic outflows regulate host galaxy gas supply, affecting early star formation and SMBH growth; however, these sources remain poorly characterized due to sensitivity and resolution limitations of current facilities.
AI.method: The paper proposes using SKA-VLBI (combining SKA-Mid and SKA-Low) to achieve sub-μJy sensitivity with milliarcsecond angular resolution for imaging and characterizing jetted AGN at z>6.
AI.result: SKA-VLBI will provide direct constraints on Doppler boosting, jet duty cycles, and jet-environment coupling at extreme redshifts, test SMBH formation models (including jet-assisted super-Eddington accretion phases), and probe cosmological geometry with high precision.
AI.conclusion: SKA-VLBI, in synergy with current and next-generation multi-band facilities, will enable unprecedented panchromatic characterization of the first jetted AGN and their host galaxies, advancing understanding of early structure formation.

title: Kinematic detection of dusty outflows from AGN: PAH kinematics of type 2 quasars with JWST/MIRI spectroscopy
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 13 pages, 12 figures
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are thought to have dusty outflows; however, unlike the gas phase, measuring the kinematics of dust is challenging. We present the detection and analysis of the kinematics of dust in five type 2 quasars (QSO2s) at $z\sim0.1$ from the Quasar Feedback (QSOFEED) sample observed with JWST/MIRI spectroscopy. We use Principal Component Analysis (PCA) tomography to produce velocity maps of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon (PAH) features, which are the smallest carbonaceous dust particles. We are then able to compare velocity maps of the PAHs with emission lines of ionised and molecular gas. We are able to produce velocity maps of the 11.3 $μ$m PAH feature, which traces large and neutral PAHs, for three out of the five objects where all three show the presence of an outflow in the PAH kinematics. This becomes particularly clear after subtracting disk kinematics, where the H$_2$ rotational transitions also show residuals consistent with an outflow. Compared to previous work with Seyfert galaxies, this work suggests that dusty outflows are more common at higher Eddington ratios, $λ_{\rm Edd}\gtrsim0.1$, in agreement with previous suggestions, although the sample size is small. We are unable to produce velocity maps for the 6.2 $μ$m PAH, which traces ionised PAHs, potentially due to differences in the intrinsic profile and/or suppression of the feature in AGN, which was seen previously in Seyfert galaxies. This reflects studies of PAH band ratios where AGN outflows have more neutral PAHs. This work demonstrates that dusty outflows may be common, particularly at high Eddington ratios, and therefore play a key role in the evolution and life cycle of AGN.

AI.tldr: This paper uses JWST/MIRI spectroscopy and PCA tomography to study the kinematics of dust (via PAH features) in five type 2 quasars (QSO2s) at z~0.1. They detect outflows in the 11.3 μm PAH (neutral/large PAHs) in three of five objects, showing dusty outflows are common at high Eddington ratios (λ_Edd≳0.1), while the 6.2 μm PAH (ionized PAHs) is suppressed, consistent with AGN outflow environments favoring neutral PAHs.
AI.motivation: While AGN are known to have dusty outflows, measuring dust kinematics has been challenging compared to gas kinematics. This work aims to fill that gap by using PAH features as kinematic tracers of dust in AGN outflows.
AI.method: JWST/MIRI spectroscopy of five QSO2s from the QSOFEED sample at z~0.1; Principal Component Analysis (PCA) tomography to produce velocity maps of PAH features (11.3 μm and 6.2 μm); comparison with ionized and molecular gas emission lines; subtraction of disk kinematics to isolate outflow residuals.
AI.result: Velocity maps of the 11.3 μm PAH (large/neutral PAHs) were produced for three of five objects, all showing outflow signatures. The 6.2 μm PAH (ionized PAHs) could not be mapped, likely due to intrinsic profile differences or suppression in AGN. H₂ rotational transitions show outflow residuals consistent with PAH kinematics. Dusty outflows appear more common at λ_Edd≳0.1.
AI.conclusion: Dusty outflows may be common in AGN, especially at high Eddington ratios, and thus likely play a key role in AGN evolution and life cycles. The suppression of ionized PAHs in outflows reflects the neutral nature of PAHs in AGN outflow environments.
